articles.title: Which Way, Democrats?
articles.author: Christian Britschgi
articles.summary: Which way, Democrats? The last couple of cycles of American electoral politics have followed the same basic pattern: Voters, angry about high prices and exhausted by the incumbent party's culture war, opt to throw the bums out. The incoming party then overreads their victory as a mandate to find new ways to hike consumer prices and launch their own aggressive culture war (and sometimes an actual war). We saw this story with Democrats in 2020, who were elected to end the madness of the first Trump administration and the COVID-19 era, and instead hiked inflation with huge amounts of unnecessary fiscal stimulus and went "full woke" on a range of cultural issues. That set the stage for Donald Trump's historic political comeback in 2024. Once in office, the current president proceeded to raise the cost of living with tariffs against the entire globe, wage a war in Iran that's restricted the global supply of oil, and go all in on a range of right-wing social issues. Two years after the much-ballyhooed " vibe shift ," Democrats are now the ones staging the historic comeback. Will they now also overread this commanding victory and overreach too? articles.summary: On a spring evening in Stockton, California, Chase Ott-Wick was strolling into a bar when a stranger stopped him. The man had heard that Chase was the guy building a new data center in town—and he wanted to say: Please don’t. “He had a beautiful home that he paid for and had been living in for years, and was concerned that his view would be disrupted,” Chase told me. But as the conversation went on, he said, it became increasingly clear that what the man really feared was something bigger. “When you turn that thing on,” Chase remembers him saying, “our lives are going to change.” The people of Stockton, which is 40 miles northeast of Silicon Valley as the crow flies, worried the harsh growl of the data center would drown out the lapping sounds of the San Joaquin River; they feared the rampant water use would turn their rolling green golf courses into a sickly bed of beige; they suspected their precious populations of migratory birds and Chinook salmon would be wiped out by pollution. articles.author: Ryan Sabalow
articles.summary: In summary Families of those killed by death row inmates react to California Gov. Gavin Newsom commuting their sentences to life in prison. They’ve lived through the worst horrors a family can endure, and they were promised their murdered loved ones would receive justice through an execution. They suffered through years, if not decades, of appeals and hearings where they were forced to hear the stories of their loved ones’ violent deaths graphically retold again and again. They watched courts — and then Gov. Gavin Newsom — suspend executions. The last one was carried out in 2006, before he was elected, despite California voters repeatedly reaffirming their support for the death penalty over the past 50 years. And then on Thursday, they learned that Newsom, in one of his final acts as governor, had commuted the death sentences to life in prison for each of the 548 murderers on death row. “These are not just numbers on a legal document,” said Sandy Friend, whose eight-year-old son was raped, tortured and murdered by a man facing a death sentence. “Each case has a family left behind. articles.author: Rogé Karma
articles.summary: Among the many gifts that Donald Trump bequeathed to Democrats ahead of the midterms was allowing them the exclusive political use of the AI backlash. Now that Democrats have decisively won control of Congress, voters will expect them to follow through on their rhetoric. The problem is that Democrats don’t actually have a plan to regulate AI. In fact, they don’t even agree on what problems need to be solved in the first place. Until recently, federal AI legislation seemed impossible until 2029 at the earliest. Trump has consistently opposed any form of AI regulation, going so far as to pressure Congress to preempt state laws. Although some Republican lawmakers have seemed more sympathetic to AI regulation, almost none would dare defy their party’s leader. Of the roughly 150 AI-focused bills that have been proposed during Trump’s second term, only one—a bill that criminalized the nonconsensual posting of sexual images, including AI-generated ones—ultimately passed. Tuesday night’s astonishing results have made AI regulation a much more realistic possibility.
